title: The Fourteen Courtesies at the Frontier
summary: A client confederation negotiates peace through polished comedy and ideal principles while a prudent ruler’s confinement policy exposes the limits of public praise.

entries.title: Congren of the Polite Bargain
entries.body:
Congren made a courteous promise conceal several incompatible expectations. Patrons repeated his witty phrases as ornaments. Actors restore the surrounding scene, showing that a memorable line may expose hypocrisy only when listeners hear who bears its actual cost.

Later accounts make Congren of the Polite Bargain the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Fourteen Courtesies at the Frontier. A frontier confederation defended the reedlands for a larger court while preserving distinct household rites. In 694 a ruler celebrated for avoiding outside wars ordered itinerant households confined, calling the measure domestic order rather than violence. A polished dramatist exposed social bargaining through lovers and rival hosts, but patrons quoted his clever lines without hearing their consequences. Peace negotiators proposed fourteen principles whose general promises exceeded what signatories were willing to provide. Frontier households welcomed reduced warfare and demanded specific terms for movement, food, and independent rites. The resulting courtesies remain useful precisely where they name finite acts, and hollow where elegant language replaces the work required to carry them out.

In the connected record, [The Frontier Courtesy House](b034-the-frontier-courtesy-house.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Rite Separate from Service](b034-the-rite-separate-from-service.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether a peace settlement can protect itinerant households and frontier rites through executable terms instead of another ceremony praising the ruler’s prudence.

entries.title: The Frontier Courtesy House
entries.body:
Delegates negotiate beneath reed screens separating discussion from kitchen work. Hosts removed one screen after cooks requested to hear provisioning terms. The change revealed that a diplomatic space’s elegance had depended on people excluded from its supposedly complete conversation.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Reed Frontier Confederation
entries.body:
Households defend crossings for an outside court while preserving different rites. Patrons claim their service proves assimilation. The confederation’s accounts distinguish agreed defense from broader cultural submission, allowing cooperation without erasing internal differences.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Prudent Ruler’s Confinement
entries.body:
Officials praised avoidance of foreign war while confining itinerant households at home. Supply records document hunger and interrupted trades. The same reign can contain reduced external fighting and deliberate domestic harm, neither canceling the other through a convenient title.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Fourteen Courtesy Tiles
entries.body:
Each tile names a peace principle. Several lack a provision schedule on the reverse. Negotiators now display both faces, turning missing practical terms into visible questions instead of allowing elegant promises to appear complete simply because they fit a numbered set.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Courtesy Answered Plainly
entries.body:
After a polished proposal, a cook or carrier restates its material requirements in ordinary language. Delegates sometimes object to lost nuance. The restatement tests whether nuance describes a real distinction or conceals an expense nobody has agreed to meet.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Lovers’ Contract Comedy
entries.body:
Two lovers negotiate honestly only after servants compare their households’ hidden expectations. The comedy’s reconciliation requires changed arrangements. Patrons commission versions ending with affection alone, avoiding the practical revision that gives the original conclusion force.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Reed Screen Nest Weaver
entries.body:
Small birds weave loose reeds taken from damaged diplomatic screens. Hosts blamed theft by servants. Inspecting nests corrected the accusation and prompted repairs, illustrating how a prestigious room’s ordinary defects could become someone else’s undeserved punishment.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Itinerants’ Interrupted Circuit
entries.body:
Confined households lost access to seasonal repair customers. After release, officials called their poverty refusal to work. Earlier itineraries show skilled trades disrupted by state choice, giving present claimants evidence of losses beyond the days spent inside compounds.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Rite Separate from Service
entries.body:
Defense service does not require changing household rites unless separately agreed. The clause protects distinct practice without granting every rite immunity from specific harm claims. Its narrow scope sustains cooperation more reliably than a declaration of absolute uniformity or absolute exemption.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Peace Principles Feast
entries.body:
Delegates announced fourteen principles before agreeing who would pay for return journeys. Several small households stayed stranded. Kitchen accounts preserve that contradiction, showing the limits of a settlement celebrated through the generosity of its opening ceremony.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Courtesy Host’s Broken Seat
entries.body:
A seat repaired repeatedly supported delegates excluded from the formal table. Its wear maps a secondary negotiation conducted outside the official record. Curators seek royal furniture, overlooking this ordinary object’s evidence of who was present but not officially counted.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Fourteenth Silence
entries.body:
Negotiators leave a pause after the last principle for unmet practical objections. Patrons want music immediately. The silence gives less polished speakers a chance to name costs before celebration makes questioning the settlement appear disrespectful.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Confined Trades’ Accounts
entries.body:
Accounts record lost tools, customers, and seasonal opportunities beside confinement dates. Their specificity supports restitution without claiming every later difficulty had one cause. Courts must examine actual pathways of harm instead of either dismissing or romanticizing a whole population’s history.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Courtesy Tiles’ Unequal Damp
entries.body:
Tiles bearing unprovided food terms dampen near the basin, while purely ceremonial ones remain dry. Different glazes explain some variation. Witnesses investigate the remaining pattern and the actual shortages separately, refusing to substitute a manifestation for provisioning.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Frontier Reed Screen Making
entries.body:
Screen makers use graded reeds to shade rooms without blocking air. Diplomats commission elaborate dense patterns that worsen heat. Craftspeople insist on testing comfort, making useful design part of negotiation rather than treating prestigious decoration as automatically superior.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Peace That Includes Return
entries.body:
Itinerant claimants demand routes, tools, and workshop access within the settlement. Delegates offer general liberty. The hearing seeks terms that turn that valuable principle into a possible journey home, preserving its aspiration by refusing to mistake it for completed action.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
